attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his 2025 predictions post, listed in the high-confidence section.

semantics.note: Keeps his definition of truly driverless, both 'mainly' qualifiers, the human-driver clause and the end-of-2025 horizon. The firm 'will' makes this a scored forecast.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. It keeps both meanings of 'West' and treats 'mainly' as unweighted. The result turns on those undefined readings.

evidence.note: Baidu's own disclosure lists fully driverless service in many Chinese mainland cities. That tells against a Western concentration, but the 22-city footprint mixes deployment stages and there is no Western comparison.
Waymo says its system handles rain and fog. That is a capability claim, not the weather mix of actual service, and winter work is still in testing.
Five new Waymo cities run without riders until next year. This shows announced markets were not public 2025 service.
3.45M US professional truck drivers in 2025 supports the human-driver clause. It says nothing on robotaxi geography or weather.

reviews.rationale: The human-driver part is supported. The packet has no end-of-2025 public-service city count and no ride split by region or weather. Baidu's Chinese footprint challenges the 'West' part on one reading, but without Western comparison data it is not clearly contradicted. Mixed needs a clear contradiction, so this stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own retrospective assessment of his own forecasting record.

semantics.note: Accurately states the self-assessment: largely right on technical and economic limits, wrong about investors.

contract.note: Through-2024 scope and an inventory-based test are reasonable. The set covered by 'largely' is unbounded, so the result depends on how that set is drawn.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement confirms a $6.6B round at a $157B valuation, the event behind his investor admission. It does not speak to the broader record.

reviews.rationale: The funding round behind the investor admission is confirmed. The main claim, that his technical and economic predictions were largely on target, would need a scored inventory of those predictions, and the packet has none. His own self-assessment cannot prove itself, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in the high-confidence section of his 2025 post.

semantics.note: Keeps all three parts (consumption rises, it stays a major problem, few companies are transparent) and the calendar-2025 horizon. The firm 'will' makes it scored.

contract.note: The reading is fair overall. The requirement to isolate generative AI from other AI workloads is stricter than his words, which do not specify that, so AI-focused data-centre figures are a fair basis.

evidence.note: IEA: electricity use by AI-focused data centres rose 50% in 2025, and it notes grid, affordability and pushback strains. A close proxy that is not generative-AI only.
FMTI: 10 of 13 major developers disclosed no key environmental information, including energy. This supports 'few transparent', though it covers training only.
Google published a per-prompt inference energy figure. One firm's partial disclosure leaves disclosers a small minority.
A Maryland state consumer advocate documents 2025 data-centre-driven capacity shortfalls and cost burdens, supporting 'major problem'. It covers data centres broadly.

reviews.rationale: All three parts point the same way. AI data-centre electricity use rose sharply in 2025. Grid and affordability burdens were documented. Most assessed developers disclosed no energy data, and Google's inference figure still leaves disclosers a minority. Nothing in the packet contradicts the forecast. The main caveat is that the figures cover AI broadly rather than generative AI alone.
